bib.title: Recent Neural Methods on Slot Filling and Intent Classification for Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems: A Survey
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:2011.00564v1 [cs.CL], 1 Nov 2020); the PDF text prints no venue, only a Creative Commons licence notice. COLING 2020 is not stated in the text.

question: How have neural models for slot filling and intent classification in task-oriented dialogue evolved, how do they compare, and what challenges remain?
contributions: Survey of three neural architecture families for SF and IC: independent, joint, and transfer learning models
Comparison tables of reported performance on ATIS and SNIPS

results.claim: Joint models nearly 'solve' ATIS and SNIPS given sufficient in-domain training data (survey conclusion).
results.setup: Survey conclusion over reported results on ATIS and SNIPS, single-turn English
results.quote: Empirical results have shown that most joint models nearly ”solve” widely used datasets, ATIS and SNIPS, given suﬃcient in-domain training data.

results.claim: When enough in-domain data exists, SF and IC performance on ATIS and SNIPS is saturated; authors say further leaderboard chasing is not worth it.
results.quote: When suﬃciently large in-domain training data is available, the SF and IC performance in ATIS and SNIPS is already saturated.

results.claim: Models have merely solved the datasets, not SF/IC or NLU in general.
results.setup: Sec 6, citing Bechet and Raymond 2018 and Niu and Penn 2019 that ATIS is simple
results.quote: it does not mean these models have solved SF and IC, or NLU problems in general, rather that the model has merely solved the datasets.

results.claim: Best reported ATIS slot F1 in Table 3 (BERT + intent gate, Zhang et al. 2019).
results.table: Table 3, row Zhang et al. (2019) BERT + Intent-Gate, column ATIS Slot F1

results.claim: Same model: ATIS intent accuracy 99.76 and SNIPS slot F1 98.78, intent 98.96.
results.table: Table 3, row Zhang et al. (2019), column ATIS Intent Acc/Err
results.note: SNIPS slot F1 98.78; SNIPS intent 98.96 (same row)

results.claim: Multi-task learning helps most over single-task learning when target-domain data is scarce; benefit shrinks as data grows.
results.source: Jaech et al. 2016; Hakkani-Tur et al. 2016; Louvan and Magnini 2019
results.setup: Transfer learning with source domains and a limited-data target domain; cited Jaech 2016, Hakkani-Tur 2016, Louvan and Magnini 2019. No numbers given.
results.quote: Results have shown that MTL is particularly eﬀective relative to single-task learning (STL) when the data in DT is scarce and the beneﬁts over STL diminish as more data is available.

results.claim: Generative models are relatively better than discriminative ones when data is scarce.
results.source: Raymond and Riccardi 2007; Yogatama et al. 2017
results.quote: have shown that a generative model is relatively better than a discriminative model in a situation where data is scarce.

results.claim: Neural SF/IC models are data hungry; transfer, zero-shot and few-shot evaluation needs more work and room for improvement is large.
results.setup: Sec 6 Portable and Data Efficient Models
results.quote: as neural models are data hungry, more work is still needed on transfer learning scenarios, where evaluation is carried out with less or without labeled data (zero-shot) for a particular target domain.

results.claim: Zero-shot cross-lingual and few-shot SF still have large room for improvement.
results.quote: the room for improvement for these scenarios is still large.

results.claim: Pre-train/fine-tune and MTL both improve performance when target-domain data is limited; fine-tuning is more prone to forgetting.
results.setup: Takeaways on scaling to new domains
results.quote: Both data driven methods, MTL and pre-train ﬁne tuning, improve performance when data in DT is limited.

results.claim: With no target annotation, zero-shot is the choice, at the cost of providing slot/intent descriptions.
results.quote: the choice is zero-shot approaches with the expense of providing meta-information such as slot and intent descriptions.

results.claim: ATIS is skewed: more than 70% of intents are flight search.
results.quote: more than 70% of the intent is a ﬂight search.

results.claim: Bidirectional Jordan RNN reached 93.89 F1 on ATIS slot filling, about +1 F1 over CRF.
results.quote: best score of 93.89 F1 for SF

results.claim: BERT joint model (Chen et al. 2019) on SNIPS: slot F1 97.00, intent 98.60; ATIS slot F1 96.10, intent 97.50.
results.table: Table 3, row Chen et al. (2019) Transformer (BERT), column SNIPS Slot F1

limits: Survey only: no new experiments; all numbers are reported from other papers and not re-run or normalised.
Table 3 mixes models with and without gold NE features and different splits; F1 scores do not show where models differ (authors leave analysis to future work).
Covers up to mid-2020: no LLM or prompting methods; ATIS/SNIPS saturation claim is about pre-LLM fine-tuned neural models.
Venue not printed in the PDF text.
practices: When computational power is not an issue, fine-tune a pre-trained model such as BERT for maximum SF and IC performance (Sec 4 takeaways).
Do not chase ATIS/SNIPS leaderboards when in-domain data is sufficient (Sec 4 takeaways).

With limited target data use MTL or pre-train and fine-tune; with many domains prefer fine-tuning or expert-based adaptation for training time; with no target annotation use zero-shot with slot descriptions (Sec 5 takeaways).
Evaluate in low-resource, zero-shot, cross-lingual and multi-intent scenarios rather than only fixed splits (Sec 6).

terms.definition: token-level sequence tagging, assigning a slot label to each token of the utterance
a classification task over utterances, assigning the correct intent label to the whole utterance
new intents and slots regularly added to a system, requiring methods to train for new domains with limited or no labeled data
